title: A Class Purpose and the Promotion of Student Flourishing
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Using summer reflection, Stuart asks what his courses are fundamentally about and answers with a purpose statement: becoming better readers, writers, thinkers, and people. He admits he rarely referred to it after September and that his ideas behind each term were vague. He then spells out a strategy for each: teaching grade-level complex texts with scaffolding plus recreational reading, a mix of grammar, formal, and informal writing, debates to bridge students' everyday arguing with academic thinking via Graff, and explicit character instruction drawn from Esquith and KIPP's seven strengths. The essay is a candid mid-career attempt to give a class a coherent purpose beyond content coverage.
points: A class needs an explicit purpose that answers the 'So what?' question of its significance in students' lives, and it must be revisited all year to matter.
Struggling readers should still be taught grade-level complex texts with heavy scaffolding, paired with choice reading for enjoyment.
Gerald Graff's idea that students already argue intellectually outside school offers a bridge to academic thinking, which Stuart builds through frequent debates.
Character can be taught through explicit instruction and consistent modeling, using KIPP's seven strengths as a concrete list.
quotes: Essentially, I’m trying to answer the “So what?” question of my course. What is its significance to a student’s life? Why does it matter?

At the end of my courses, I want them all to have grown in their aptitudes for reading, writing, and thinking, and I also want them to have developed character. Though I still agree with this purpose statement for my students and apart from a few emphatic references to this sentence at the start of the year, I rarely mentioned it after September; few of my students could probably tell you today what the core purpose of our class was during the 2011-2012 school year.

The alternative to this is allowing Johnny to solely read books of his choosing or books that are slightly above his abilities; unfortunately, the college/career world will not make such concessions for him; inevitably, my friend Johnny will be faced with complex texts well beyond him. Lowering the standards for Johnny defeats all of my purposes as a teacher.

In other words, Graff helped me see that my students will become more comfortable in the argumentative cultures of the various academic disciplines when they see them as akin to the argumentative cultures they are already comfortable in. This coming school year, I’m going to spend the first month attempting to more fully achieve this bridging with my students, but in the past year I saw great success in this area simply by repeatedly arranging for frequent debates in our history and English classes.

So even as a beginning teacher in Baltimore, I knew I wanted my students to become more than better readers, writers, and thinkers. I knew that academically and intellectually strong people can still be horrible friends and miserable coworkers if they lack the ability to be nice or the grit to work hard.

The seven strengths — grit, zest, optimism, self-control, social intelligence, gratitude, and curiosity — were chosen from a list of 24 human virtues compiled by Peterson and Seligman. Though all 24 of the virtues are found to lead to “happy, engaged, and meaningful lives,” KIPP chooses to focus on the seven that are most closely linked with college and career success.
